questions.q: The glycoprotein spikes, such as haemagglutinin, on the envelope of the influenza virus mainly help the virus to:
o: Attach to specific receptors on host cells
questions.x: Envelope spikes are the attachment proteins: haemagglutinin binds receptors on cells of the respiratory tract. The genome is inside the capsid, and viruses make no ATP.

questions.q: Hepatitis C, which is common in Pakistan, spreads mainly through:
o: Food and water contaminated with faeces
Contaminated blood, for example reused syringes
questions.x: The hepatitis C virus is blood-borne, as is the hepatitis B virus, so reused syringes, unscreened blood and unsterile instruments spread it. Faecally contaminated food and water spread other hepatitis viruses instead.

questions.q: A person breathes in oxygen gas labelled with the heavy isotope oxygen-18. In respiration, this labelled oxygen first appears in:
questions.x: Molecular oxygen is used only at the end of the electron transport chain, where it is reduced to water. The oxygen in respired carbon dioxide comes from the substrate and water, not from oxygen gas.

questions.q: In alcoholic fermentation by yeast, pyruvate is first:
o: Converted to acetyl CoA in the mitochondria
Joined with oxaloacetate to form citrate
Decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which is then reduced to ethanol
questions.x: Yeast removes carbon dioxide from pyruvate to give acetaldehyde, then NADH reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol. Direct reduction to lactic acid happens in muscle, not yeast.

questions.q: In aerobic respiration, less than half of the energy in glucose is trapped in ATP. The rest of the energy is:
questions.x: Energy not captured in ATP is released as heat; in mammals and birds this heat helps keep body temperature up.

questions.q: The glycosidic bond in lactose links:
o: Glucose to fructose by an α(1→2) bond
Two glucose units by an α(1→4) bond
Galactose to glucose by a β(1→4) bond
Galactose to fructose by a β(1→6) bond
questions.x: Lactose is galactose joined to glucose by a β(1→4) glycosidic bond. Glucose–fructose α(1→2) is sucrose, and two glucose units α(1→4) is maltose.

questions.q: Which pairing of a polysaccharide with its role is correct?
questions.x: Animals store glucose as glycogen. Starch is the plant store, cellulose forms plant cell walls, and chitin is a structural polysaccharide of arthropods and fungi.

questions.q: In a membrane glycolipid, the lipid portion is:
o: Projecting outside the cell as an identity marker
Embedded in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer
questions.x: The fatty acid tails of a glycolipid sit among the tails of the bilayer, anchoring it. Only its sugar chain projects outside the cell.

questions.q: Chylomicrons are lipoproteins that carry fat absorbed from the:
questions.x: Digested fat absorbed by cells of the small intestine is packed into chylomicrons, which pass into the lymph and then the blood.

questions.q: The digestive enzyme pepsin breaks down proteins by:
questions.x: Pepsin is a protease that uses water to break peptide bonds, splitting proteins into smaller peptides. Glycosidic bonds are broken by carbohydrases such as amylase.

questions.q: The genetic information carried by DNA is stored in:
o: The number of its phosphate groups
The type of sugar it contains
The width of its double helix
questions.x: The sugar–phosphate backbone and the helix width are the same in all DNA. Only the order of the bases varies, and this sequence carries the information.

questions.q: The two long hydrocarbon tails of a phospholipid molecule are:
o: Hydrophilic, so they dissolve in water
Hydrophobic, so they turn away from water
Polar, so they bond to the phosphate head
questions.x: The fatty acid tails are non-polar hydrocarbon chains, so they are hydrophobic and point away from water. Only the phosphate-containing head is hydrophilic.

questions.q: The purine bases present in RNA are:
questions.x: Adenine and guanine are the double-ringed purines in both DNA and RNA. Cytosine and uracil are the pyrimidines of RNA.

questions.q: The general formula of the glucose polymers starch, glycogen and cellulose can be written as:
questions.x: Each glucose unit (C6H12O6) loses one water molecule when it joins the chain, so each unit in the polymer is C6H10O5.

questions.q: A single small unit that can join with many similar units to form a large molecule is called a:
questions.x: A monomer is the repeating building block; many monomers joined together make a polymer (a macromolecule). Isomers are molecules with the same formula but different structures.

questions.q: The genetic code is non-overlapping. This means that:
o: Each codon codes for more than one amino acid
Each nucleotide is part of only one codon
Codons are separated by spacer bases
Two genes can never share a chromosome
questions.x: In a non-overlapping code, successive codons do not share bases: each base is read in just one triplet.

questions.q: During cell division, chromatin coils up tightly into short, thick chromosomes. The main advantage of this is that:
o: Genes can be transcribed more quickly
Chromosomes can be separated without tangling or breaking
questions.x: Long thin chromatin would tangle and break when pulled apart; compact chromosomes are moved easily by the spindle. Condensed chromatin is actually less active in transcription.

questions.q: In the cells of higher plants, the mitotic spindle forms without centrioles. Such a spindle, having no asters at its poles, is called:
questions.x: Asters form around centrioles, which higher plant cells lack, so their spindle is anastral. Animal cells, with centrioles, form an astral spindle.

questions.q: During cytokinesis, a plant cell divides by forming a:
o: Cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two
Cell plate across the middle of the cell
Pair of new centrioles at the equator
questions.x: A rigid wall cannot be pinched in, so plant cells build a cell plate from Golgi vesicles that grows outwards into a new wall. Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow.

questions.q: In grafting experiments on the single-celled alga Acetabularia, the cap that finally forms, after any first mixed cap is removed, matches the species that supplied the:
questions.x: Hämmerling showed that the cap formed depends on the nucleus, not the stalk, proving that the nucleus holds the information controlling the cell's form.

questions.q: Small areas of a plant cell wall where secondary wall material is not laid down, so that the wall stays thin, are called:
questions.x: Pits are thin regions in the secondary wall, usually opposite pits of neighbouring cells, which help water and solutes pass. Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic strands passing through the wall.

questions.q: The pineal gland is a small structure that belongs to the:
questions.x: The pineal gland arises from the roof of the diencephalon, which is part of the forebrain. The cerebellum and medulla oblongata belong to the hindbrain.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes a reflex action from a voluntary action?
o: A reflex always uses a gland as the effector
A reflex does not need a conscious decision before the response
A reflex always involves the cerebral cortex
A reflex is slower than a voluntary action
questions.x: Reflexes are automatic and involuntary: the response is produced without waiting for a conscious decision. They are usually faster than voluntary actions and can use muscles or glands.

questions.q: The ankle-jerk reflex, in which tapping the Achilles tendon makes the calf muscle contract, is classified as a:
questions.x: Like the knee jerk, the ankle jerk is a stretch reflex: the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron in the spinal cord. It is inborn, so it is not conditioned.

questions.q: When acetylcholine binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane of a neuron, the immediate effect is that:
o: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the postsynaptic membrane
Ion channels open, Na+ enters and the membrane depolarises
questions.x: The receptors are linked to ion channels; when they open, Na+ enters and depolarises the postsynaptic membrane. Ca2+ entry into the knob happens earlier, before release.

questions.q: Nerve fibres that carry information about a spinal reflex up to the brain run in the:
o: White matter of the spinal cord
Ventral roots of the spinal nerves
Central canal of the spinal cord
questions.x: Long tracts of myelinated fibres in the white matter carry impulses up and down the spinal cord, letting the brain learn of the stimulus. Ventral roots carry motor fibres out, and the central canal holds cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.q: When reflexes are divided into monosynaptic and polysynaptic types, the basis of the division is the:
o: Part of the central nervous system where the reflex is integrated
Whether the reflex is inborn or learned
Type of effector that gives the response
Number of synapses between neurons in the reflex arc
questions.x: Monosynaptic arcs have one synapse (sensory neuron directly to motor neuron); polysynaptic arcs have interneurons and so more synapses. The spinal/cranial division depends on the centre, and conditioned/unconditioned on learning.

questions.q: An action potential spreads along a non-myelinated axon because:
o: Local currents from the depolarised region bring the next part of the membrane to threshold
Neurotransmitter is released at every point along the axon
The axon membrane contracts in waves
The sodium–potassium pump pushes the impulse forward
questions.x: Positive charge flows from the active region to the neighbouring resting region, depolarising it to threshold, so a new action potential arises there.

questions.q: The level to which the membrane must be depolarised to trigger an action potential is called the:
questions.x: Once depolarisation reaches the threshold potential, an action potential fires. The resting potential is the starting value at rest.

questions.q: Some nerve gases and organophosphate insecticides are deadly because they:
o: Act as cofactors for nerve enzymes
Increase the activity of nerve enzymes
questions.x: These poisons bind permanently to acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine is not broken down and nerve impulses go out of control.

questions.q: An enzyme–substrate complex is not always converted into products. It can also:
o: Break apart into free enzyme and unchanged substrate
questions.x: Binding is by weak bonds and is reversible, so some complexes simply separate again before any reaction happens.

questions.q: After the enzyme–substrate complex has formed, the next step is that:
o: The substrate is changed into product while still bound, forming an enzyme–product complex
The enzyme is copied to form a new enzyme
The enzyme turns into a coenzyme
questions.x: The sequence is E + S → ES → EP → E + P: the substrate is converted on the enzyme, and then the products are released.

questions.q: The substance on which an enzyme acts is called its:
questions.x: The substrate binds to the active site and is changed into products. A cofactor helps the enzyme, and an inhibitor slows it.

questions.q: When Fox placed proteinoids in water, they formed tiny cell-like spheres known as:
questions.x: Proteinoids in water gather into microspheres, which have a boundary and can swell, shrink and bud. Coacervates are the related droplets described by Oparin.

questions.q: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, who proposed the inheritance of acquired characters, was a:
questions.x: Lamarck was a French naturalist. Weismann was German, Lyell an English geologist and Mendel an Austrian monk.

questions.q: Darwin explained the large, brightly coloured tail of the male peacock by:
o: Use and disuse of the tail feathers
Protection of the male from predators
Inheritance of feathers damaged during fights
Sexual selection, as females prefer to mate with males having showy tails
questions.x: Darwin proposed sexual selection: traits that make males more attractive to females increase mating success, even if they do not help survival.

questions.q: Two male deer of the same species fighting for a female is an example of:
questions.x: Both deer belong to one species, so this is intraspecific struggle. Such contests decide which males pass on their genes.

questions.q: Inhibin, which reduces the secretion of FSH in the male, is produced by the:
questions.x: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which acts on the anterior pituitary to lower FSH. Leydig cells secrete testosterone.

questions.q: Compared with a sperm, a human ovum is:
o: Much larger and non-motile, with stored food
Smaller and moves by a flagellum
Of the same size but has no nucleus
Larger and moves by many cilia
questions.x: The ovum is a large, non-motile cell with stored nutrients in its cytoplasm. The sperm is tiny and swims using its tail (flagellum).

questions.q: At mid-cycle, which pituitary hormones show a sharp peak at the same time?
questions.x: Both LH and FSH rise sharply at mid-cycle, LH much more than FSH. Oestrogen and progesterone are ovarian, not pituitary, hormones.

questions.q: When the elbow is bent (flexed) to lift the forearm:
o: The triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes
Both biceps and triceps contract fully
The biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
Both biceps and triceps relax fully
questions.x: The biceps is the flexor of the elbow; it contracts and pulls the forearm up while its antagonist, the triceps, relaxes. The triceps contracts to straighten (extend) the arm.

questions.q: Which of the following increases the risk of an attack of gout?
o: Eating a diet low in purines
questions.x: Alcohol, especially beer, raises blood uric acid and can trigger gout attacks. Plenty of water helps the kidneys remove uric acid, and a low-purine diet lowers it.

questions.q: A student claims arthritis affects only elderly people. The correct reply is that arthritis:
o: Affects only the joints of the hands
Can occur at any age, including in children
questions.x: Although osteoarthritis is common in older people, forms of arthritis can affect any age, including children. It may involve many different joints and has several causes, not only infection.

questions.q: The sacrum, which joins the vertebral column to the pelvic girdle, is formed by the fusion of:
questions.x: The sacrum consists of five fused sacral vertebrae. It forms the back of the pelvis and articulates with the two hip bones.

questions.q: The movements possible at a hinge joint are:
o: Rotation around the long axis only
Bending and straightening (flexion and extension) in one plane
questions.x: A hinge joint works like a door hinge: it bends and straightens in one plane only. Rotation is the movement of a pivot joint, and movement in all directions belongs to a ball-and-socket joint.

questions.q: A property of cardiac muscle that skeletal muscle lacks is that cardiac muscle:
o: Is attached to bones by tendons
Contracts rhythmically on its own, without a nerve impulse
questions.x: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: the heartbeat starts within the muscle itself. Skeletal muscle contracts only when a motor nerve stimulates it. Both contain actin and myosin and are striated.

questions.q: Smooth muscle is also known as:
questions.x: Smooth muscle shows no cross-striations, so it is called unstriated (non-striated) muscle. It is also involuntary.

questions.q: In a relaxed sarcomere, the paler region seen at the centre of the dark A band is the:
questions.x: The H zone is the central part of the A band that thin filaments do not reach in a relaxed sarcomere, so it looks paler than the overlap regions beside it. The I band lies outside the A band.

questions.q: Which of these crosses can produce a daughter with hemophilia?
questions.x: A hemophilic daughter needs Xʰ from both parents, so the father must be XʰY and the mother must carry Xʰ. Only XᴴXʰ × XʰY fits.

questions.q: Which of the following was a key reason for the success of Mendel's experiments?
o: He could see genes on chromosomes under the microscope
He worked on Drosophila, which breeds quickly
He studied one or two characters at a time and analysed large numbers of offspring mathematically
He chose characters whose genes were linked on one chromosome
questions.x: Mendel followed a few clear contrasting characters, used pure lines, counted large numbers and analysed the ratios. Genes and chromosomes were unknown to him, Drosophila was Morgan's organism, and linked genes would have hidden independent assortment.

questions.q: How many sex chromosomes are present in a normal human body cell?
questions.x: Each body cell has one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in females and XY in males. The other 44 are autosomes.

questions.q: Reciprocal crosses in peas (tall female × dwarf male, and dwarf female × tall male) gave identical F1 results. This showed that:
o: The tall allele is carried only by the male
It did not matter which parent, male or female, contributed each allele
The dwarf allele is lost during fertilisation
Height in peas is controlled by the environment
questions.x: Identical results from reciprocal crosses show that both parents contribute equally and the trait does not depend on the sex of the parent. The dwarf allele is not lost; it reappears in the F2.

questions.q: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds fully for two genes that are located:
o: Close together on the same chromosome
questions.x: Genes on different (non-homologous) chromosomes are shuffled independently at metaphase I. Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and tend to stay together.

questions.q: The protein framework that holds homologous chromosomes closely paired during synapsis is the:
questions.x: The synaptonemal complex forms between homologues during synapsis and keeps them tightly paired so crossing over can occur. The spindle moves chromosomes later in division.

questions.q: Recombination frequencies are 12% between genes X and Y, 7% between Y and Z, and 5% between X and Z. Which gene lies in the middle?
o: The order cannot be worked out
questions.x: The largest distance (X–Y, 12) is between the two outer genes, and 5 + 7 = 12. So the order is X–Z–Y, with Z in the middle.

questions.q: A pea plant RrYy produces gametes in which proportions?
o: Only RY and ry, in equal proportions
RY, Ry, rY and ry in equal proportions (1 : 1 : 1 : 1)
RY and ry more often than Ry and rY
RY, Ry, rY and ry in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio
questions.x: Because the two genes assort independently, each allele of one gene combines equally often with each allele of the other, giving four gamete types in equal numbers. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is the F2 phenotype ratio, not a gamete ratio.

questions.q: Infection and swelling of the tonsils is called:
questions.x: Inflammation of the tonsils is tonsillitis. Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, and elephantiasis is caused by blocked lymph vessels.

questions.q: Which pairing of a heart chamber with a vessel connected to it is correct?
questions.x: The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, the pulmonary veins enter the left atrium, and the venae cavae enter the right atrium.

questions.q: When the muscle of the ventricles relaxes and the ventricles refill with blood, they are said to be in:
questions.x: Relaxation of a heart chamber is diastole, and contraction is systole. The chambers fill with blood during diastole.

questions.q: By the classic textbook threshold, a person has high blood pressure (hypertension) when the reading stays at or above about:
questions.x: About 120/80 mmHg is normal for a young adult. In the classic textbook definition, a reading that stays at about 140/90 mmHg or more is taken as hypertension.

questions.q: A baby is breast-fed and was also given the BCG vaccine at birth. The baby therefore has:
o: Natural active immunity and artificial passive immunity
Natural passive immunity and artificial active immunity
questions.x: Antibodies received in breast milk give natural passive immunity. The vaccine makes the baby's own immune system respond, which is artificial active immunity.

questions.q: Why is the T-cell arm of specific defence described as 'cell-mediated'?
o: Antibodies dissolved in plasma do the work
Red blood cells carry the antigens away
The skin and mucous membranes block entry
T cells act directly on other cells themselves
questions.x: In cell-mediated immunity T cells act themselves, for example by killing infected cells, rather than through antibodies released into body fluids.

questions.q: Unlike B cells, T cells recognise an antigen only when it is:
o: Bound to a red blood cell
Displayed on the surface of a body cell
questions.x: T-cell receptors bind antigen fragments presented on the surface of body cells, such as macrophages or infected cells. B cells can bind free antigen directly.

questions.q: A heavy smoker becomes breathless very quickly when climbing stairs. Which two effects of smoking together best explain this?
o: Nicotine slows the heart, and tar widens the bronchi
Tar increases the number of alveoli, and carbon monoxide raises haemoglobin's oxygen release
Carbon monoxide lowers the oxygen carried by blood, and damaged alveoli reduce the surface for gas exchange
Nicotine lowers blood pressure, and cilia beat faster
questions.x: Carboxyhaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, and breakdown of alveolar walls reduces the area for diffusion; both cut oxygen supply to the muscles. Nicotine actually speeds the heart, and tar does not widen airways.

questions.q: Deoxygenated blood returning from the body tissues and arriving at the lungs normally has an oxygen partial pressure of about:
questions.x: Blood arriving in the pulmonary capillaries has a pO₂ of about 40 mm Hg, while alveolar air is about 100 mm Hg; this gradient drives oxygen into the blood. 160 mm Hg is the pO₂ of atmospheric air.

questions.q: The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is S-shaped (sigmoid) because:
o: Haemoglobin can carry only one oxygen molecule
Oxygen binds to the globin chains rather than the haem groups
Binding of one oxygen molecule makes it easier for the next ones to bind
Carbon dioxide is always bound to haemoglobin at the same sites
questions.x: After the first oxygen binds, the shape of haemoglobin changes so the remaining haem groups take up oxygen more easily (cooperative binding). This gives the curve its steep middle section and S shape.

questions.q: Which statement about swallowing is correct?
o: It is entirely voluntary from the mouth to the stomach
It is entirely a reflex and cannot be started at will
It depends on gravity, so it cannot happen when lying down
It starts voluntarily, then continues as an automatic reflex once food reaches the pharynx
questions.x: The tongue pushes the bolus back voluntarily; once it touches the pharynx, the swallowing reflex and then peristalsis take over. Because peristalsis moves the food, swallowing works even upside down.

questions.q: The longest part of the human alimentary canal is the:
questions.x: The small intestine is several metres long, far longer than the large intestine (about 1.5 m), which gives time and surface for digestion and absorption.

questions.q: The part of a tooth that lies hidden inside the socket of the jaw bone is the:
questions.x: The root is embedded in the jaw socket. The crown is the exposed part above the gum, and the neck is the narrow region at the gum line.

questions.q: In the control of body temperature, which pair correctly names the control centre and an effector?
questions.x: The hypothalamus compares body temperature with the set point and sends signals to effectors such as sweat glands, skin arterioles and muscles.

questions.q: A build-up of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood because of kidney failure is called:
questions.x: Uraemia means 'urine in the blood': wastes the kidneys should remove stay in the plasma. Glycosuria is glucose in urine; jaundice is due to bile pigments.

questions.q: Water reabsorbed from the collecting ducts deep in the medulla is carried away into the circulation by the:
questions.x: The vasa recta are the peritubular capillaries of the medulla, running beside loops of Henle and collecting ducts. They take up the water and solutes reabsorbed there.

questions.q: If disease destroyed the peritubular capillaries but left the glomeruli working, which result is expected?
o: Reabsorbed substances could not return to the blood, and the tubule cells would lack oxygen
Filtration in the glomeruli would stop at once
Plasma proteins would start to be filtered
The urine would become more concentrated
questions.x: Peritubular capillaries take up reabsorbed materials and supply tubule cells with oxygen and nutrients. Glomerular filtration depends on the afferent supply, so it could continue for a time.

questions.q: In a hot environment, the hypothalamus switches on the sweat glands by means of:
questions.x: Sweating is a fast response controlled by nerves from the hypothalamus. Thyroxine acts slowly on metabolic rate.

questions.q: After a person drinks extra water, urine volume rises, but the total amount of urea excreted that day stays about the same. This shows that:
o: Water output is adjusted separately from the removal of wastes
Urea is reabsorbed whenever water is drunk
The kidneys stop excreting urea when water is plentiful
Urea output depends only on how much water is drunk
questions.x: The kidneys change water output for osmoregulation while continuing to excrete the urea produced by metabolism. The two roles run side by side, one varying with intake and the other with waste production.

questions.q: On a cold day with normal drinking and little sweating, a person passes more urine than on a hot day. This is because:
o: Less water is lost as sweat, so ADH secretion is lower
Cold weather stops ADH from being made at all
Cold makes the glomeruli filter less
More water is lost through sweating in the cold
questions.x: With little water lost in sweat the blood stays dilute, so less ADH is released and the extra water leaves as urine. ADH is reduced, not stopped.

questions.q: The 'renal threshold' for glucose is:
o: The blood glucose level above which glucose begins to appear in urine
The lowest blood glucose level at which filtration stops
The amount of glucose secreted into the DCT
The blood glucose level at which insulin is released
questions.x: The PCT carriers can reabsorb only a limited amount of glucose. Once blood glucose rises past the renal threshold, the filtered glucose exceeds this capacity and the excess spills into the urine.

questions.q: The medical term for the formation of stones in the kidney is:
questions.x: 'Nephro' means kidney and 'lith' means stone. Nephritis and glomerulonephritis are inflammation; hydronephrosis is swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine.

questions.q: DNA fingerprinting compares regions of DNA that:
o: Code for the same protein in every person
Contain short sequences repeated a different number of times in different people
Are found only in red blood cells
questions.x: Non-coding regions with tandem repeats vary in the number of repeats between individuals, so cutting or amplifying them gives fragments of different lengths. This produces a band pattern unique to each person except identical twins.

questions.q: Some restriction enzymes cut both strands of DNA at exactly the same point. The fragments produced have:
o: Blunt ends with no unpaired bases
questions.x: A straight cut through both strands gives blunt ends. Sticky ends arise only when the enzyme makes staggered cuts, leaving short single-stranded overhangs.

questions.q: Liposomes used to carry genes into cells in gene therapy are:
o: Modified bacteria that infect the lungs
Tiny spheres with a lipid bilayer that can fuse with cell membranes
Small circular DNA molecules from bacteria
questions.x: A liposome is a small vesicle made of phospholipid bilayer; DNA packed inside it is delivered when the liposome fuses with the cell membrane. Small circular bacterial DNA molecules are plasmids.

questions.q: For S + O₂ → SO₂, 8 g of sulphur is burnt in 12 g of oxygen. What mass of oxygen remains unreacted? (S = 32, O = 16)
questions.x: S = 8/32 = 0.25 mol; O₂ = 12/32 = 0.375 mol. Sulphur is limiting and uses 0.25 mol O₂, leaving 0.125 mol × 32 = 4 g of O₂.

questions.q: A reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium and the product is then separated. Its percentage yield will be:
o: Exactly 100%, because the limiting reactant is used up
Less than 100%, because some reactants remain unconverted at equilibrium
More than 100%, because the reverse reaction adds product
Exactly 50%, because forward and reverse rates are equal
questions.x: At equilibrium both reactants and products are present, so the limiting reactant is not fully converted and the actual yield is below the theoretical yield. Equal rates do not mean equal amounts.

questions.q: According to the Aufbau order, the subshell that is filled immediately after 3d is:
questions.x: The order runs …3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s… After 3d (n + l = 5) comes 4p (also 5, but higher n). 4s is filled before 3d.

questions.q: A student writes the ground-state configuration of beryllium (Z = 4) as 1s² 2s¹ 2p¹. This breaks:
questions.x: The 2s orbital is lower in energy and must be filled before 2p, so the correct ground state is 1s² 2s². No orbital holds two same-spin electrons, so Pauli is not broken.

questions.q: Which pair of subshells has the same (n + l) value?
questions.x: 3d: 3 + 2 = 5 and 4p: 4 + 1 = 5. The others are 4 and 5, 4 and 5, and 4 and 5.

questions.q: The unit dm³ atm, used in one value of R, is a unit of:
questions.x: Pressure × volume = (force/area) × volume = force × distance, which is work or energy. This is why R can be given both in dm³ atm and in joules.

questions.q: When the units are kept the same, the value of R:
o: Does not depend on the amount, temperature or pressure of the gas
questions.x: R is a universal constant: in fixed units it has one value for all ideal gases under all conditions. Only a change of units changes its number.

questions.q: In calculations using Charles's law, temperatures must be in kelvin because:
o: The kelvin scale gives larger numbers that are easier to divide
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, not to Celsius temperature
Gas volume does not change with temperature in °C
Celsius temperatures can only be used for liquids
questions.x: V ∝ T holds only when T is measured from absolute zero. On the Celsius scale, 0 °C does not mean zero volume, so ratios of Celsius temperatures give wrong answers.

questions.q: The kinetic molecular theory assumes that, within one pure gas sample, every molecule has:
o: The same speed as every other molecule at a given temperature
A mass that depends on how fast it moves
The same mass and size as every other molecule
questions.x: The theory assumes that all molecules of a given gas are identical in mass and size. Their speeds vary from molecule to molecule; only the average kinetic energy is fixed by temperature.

questions.q: A crystal of potassium permanganate placed at the bottom of a beaker of still water slowly colours all the water. This shows that liquid molecules:
o: Are in constant motion, so particles spread by diffusion
Are held rigidly in fixed positions
questions.x: Without stirring, the colour spreads only because the moving water molecules jostle the ions about, i.e. diffusion. Liquid molecules do attract one another.

questions.q: Which change would NOT increase the magnitude of the lattice energy of an ionic compound?
o: Increasing the charge on the cation
Increasing the charge on the anion
Decreasing the distance between the ion centres
Increasing the radius of the ions
questions.x: Lattice energy grows with ionic charge and falls as the ions get larger and further apart, so larger radii reduce it.

questions.q: Because they have no regular long-range arrangement of particles, amorphous solids such as glass are often described as:
questions.x: An amorphous solid has the disordered arrangement of a liquid frozen in place, so it is called a supercooled liquid.

questions.q: A saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt is one in which:
o: No undissolved solid can ever be present
The dissolved ions are in equilibrium with the undissolved solid
The ionic product is less than Ksp
questions.x: In a saturated solution, solid dissolves and ions re-crystallise at equal rates, so the ionic product equals Ksp.

questions.q: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) has ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹. The equilibrium yield of NO is increased by:
questions.x: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating shifts the equilibrium to the right. Moles of gas are equal on both sides, so pressure has no effect, and a catalyst never changes the yield.

questions.q: For NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂, experiments give rate = k[NO₂]²; changing [CO] has no effect. Which mechanism fits this result?
o: NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ in a single step
NO₂ → NO + O (slow), then O + CO → CO₂ (fast)
NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (fast), then NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (slow)
NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow), then NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast)
questions.x: The slowest step decides the rate equation, so it must involve two NO₂ and no CO. A single step would give rate = k[NO₂][CO], and a slow NO₂ → NO + O step would be first order.

questions.q: A second-order reaction has k = 0.5 mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹. Which concentration of its single reactant X would make it proceed at 0.02 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹?
questions.x: [X]² = rate/k = 0.02/0.5 = 0.04, so [X] = 0.2 mol dm⁻³. Stopping at 0.04 forgets to take the square root.

questions.q: At a fixed temperature, the effect of adding a catalyst is shown on a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve by:
o: Moving the activation-energy mark to lower energy, with the curve itself unchanged
Shifting the whole curve to higher energies
Making the curve taller and narrower
Moving the activation-energy mark to higher energy
questions.x: A catalyst does not change the energies of the molecules, so the curve stays the same. It lowers Ea, so a larger area lies beyond the new Ea mark.

questions.q: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to:
o: Raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C
Raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C
questions.x: One calorie raises 1 g of water by 1 °C (about 4.184 J). The heat for 1 kg of water would be a kilocalorie.

questions.q: Which pair of changes are BOTH endothermic?
o: Combustion of ethanol and freezing of water
Condensation of steam and melting of ice
Evaporation of ethanol and sublimation of iodine
Neutralisation of an acid and respiration of glucose
questions.x: Evaporation and sublimation separate particles against their attractions, so both absorb heat. Combustion, freezing, condensation, neutralisation and respiration release heat.

questions.q: Hess's law of constant heat summation is a consequence of:
o: The first law of thermodynamics (conservation of energy)
questions.x: If two routes between the same states gave different ΔH, energy could be created by going one way and returning the other, which breaks the first law.

questions.q: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ is a redox reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced. Such a reaction is called:
questions.x: Oxygen at −1 in H₂O₂ goes partly to −2 (in H₂O) and partly to 0 (in O₂). Simultaneous oxidation and reduction of one element is disproportionation.

questions.q: The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the atoms in a neutral compound is:
o: Equal to the number of atoms
Equal to the charge on the cation
questions.x: In a neutral compound the positive and negative oxidation numbers cancel, so their sum is zero; in an ion the sum equals the ion's charge.

questions.q: The bond energy of H–Cl is 431 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of H–I is 299 kJ mol⁻¹. Which conclusion is correct?
o: HCl is less stable to heat than HI
The H–I bond is shorter than the H–Cl bond
HI decomposes into its elements on heating more easily than HCl
questions.x: A lower bond energy means the bond breaks more easily, so HI is less thermally stable. The weaker H–I bond is also longer, because iodine is a larger atom.

questions.q: Water has a bond angle of 104.5°. When a water molecule accepts a proton to become H₃O⁺, its bond angle:
o: Increases, because oxygen now has one lone pair instead of two
Decreases, because oxygen now has more bond pairs
Stays the same, because both are based on four electron pairs
Increases to 120°, because H₃O⁺ becomes trigonal planar
questions.x: In H₃O⁺ one lone pair of oxygen is used to bond H⁺, leaving one lone pair (pyramidal, about 107°). Water has two lone pairs, which squeeze the angle to 104.5°.

questions.q: Magnesium burnt in air forms some magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂. When water is added to the ash, a gas with a sharp smell is given off. The products are:
questions.x: Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O → 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃; the pungent gas is ammonia, with nitrogen still at −3.

questions.q: The block to which an element belongs is decided by:
o: The number of neutrons in its nucleus
The subshell that receives the last (differentiating) electron
The number of shells in its atom
questions.x: s-, p-, d- and f-blocks are named after the subshell being filled by the last electron. The number of shells gives the period, not the block.

questions.q: Iron(III) compounds are often more stable than iron(II) compounds. In terms of electronic structure, this is because:
o: Fe³⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
Fe³⁺ keeps both of its 4s electrons
questions.x: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ while Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵, a half-filled subshell with extra stability. Fe²⁺ actually has 4 unpaired electrons, and both 4s electrons are lost in Fe³⁺.

questions.q: In methane, CH₄, the four C–H bonds point towards the corners of a:
o: Regular tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5°
Straight line, with a bond angle of 180°
questions.x: A carbon atom with four single bonds (sp³) has its bonds directed to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, 109.5° apart.

questions.q: When most organic compounds are burnt completely in excess air, they give:
questions.x: Organic compounds contain carbon and hydrogen, which burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O. CO forms only when oxygen is limited.

questions.q: One of the pentene isomers has the structure CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂. Its systematic name is:
questions.x: The longest chain containing the double bond has four carbons. Numbering from the CH₂= end puts C=C at carbon 1 and the methyl at carbon 2.

questions.q: The reaction C₂H₅Br + KOH(aq) → C₂H₅OH + KBr is classified as:
questions.x: The –OH group replaces the bromine atom on the same carbon, so it is a (nucleophilic) substitution. With alcoholic KOH, elimination to ethene would occur instead.

questions.q: Removing a hydrogen from the middle carbon of propane gives the substituent (CH₃)₂CH–. Its common name is:
questions.x: (CH₃)₂CH– has three carbons and is attached through the middle carbon, so it is isopropyl. n-propyl, CH₃CH₂CH₂–, is attached through an end carbon.

questions.q: Propyne reacts with excess hydrogen bromide (two moles). The final product is:
questions.x: Each addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H goes to the carbon with more hydrogens and Br to C2. The first addition gives 2-bromopropene, the second puts another Br on C2.

questions.q: One mole of ethane is chlorinated until all its hydrogen atoms are replaced, giving C₂Cl₆. How many moles of HCl are formed?
questions.x: C₂H₆ + 6Cl₂ → C₂Cl₆ + 6HCl: each hydrogen replaced produces one HCl. Ethane has six hydrogens, so 6 mol HCl.

questions.q: Towards addition reactions, benzene compared with ethene is:
questions.x: Ethene adds bromine and hydrogen halides easily at room temperature. Benzene adds only under harsh conditions, because addition would destroy its stable delocalised π system.

questions.q: How many open-chain alkynes have the molecular formula C₄H₆?
questions.x: Only but-1-yne (CH≡CCH₂CH₃) and but-2-yne (CH₃C≡CCH₃) are possible; a four-carbon chain with a triple bond cannot branch.

questions.q: Ignoring cis–trans isomers, which alkyl halide gives only one alkene when heated with alcoholic KOH?
questions.x: In 3-bromopentane both β-carbons are equivalent, so only pent-2-ene forms. Each of the others has two different β-carbons and gives two alkenes, for example but-1-ene and but-2-ene from 2-bromobutane.

questions.q: When burnt in air, phenol and ethanol differ in that:
o: Phenol burns with a smoky (sooty) flame, while ethanol burns with a clean blue flame
Ethanol burns with a sooty flame, while phenol does not burn
Both burn with a clean blue flame
Phenol burns with a clean flame, while ethanol gives soot
questions.x: Phenol is aromatic with a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, so combustion is incomplete and the flame is smoky. Ethanol burns almost completely with a pale blue flame.

questions.q: The general formula of saturated monohydric alcohols is:
questions.x: A saturated monohydric alcohol is an alkane with one H replaced by –OH, so it is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH (for example C₂H₅OH when n = 2).

questions.q: Besides the ester, the other product of the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is:
questions.x: Acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water. Hydrogen chloride is produced only when an acid chloride is used in place of the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: 2.9 g of propanone (M = 58) is completely reduced to propan-2-ol (M = 60). What mass of propan-2-ol is formed?
questions.x: Moles of propanone = 2.9/58 = 0.05 mol, giving 0.05 mol of propan-2-ol = 0.05 × 60 = 3.0 g. The mass rises slightly because two H atoms are added.

questions.q: X, C₄H₈O, gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. On oxidation it gives 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH. X is:
questions.x: The silver mirror shows X is an aldehyde, and oxidation keeps the carbon skeleton, so X is (CH₃)₂CHCHO. Butanal would give butanoic acid; butanone is a ketone and 2-methylpropan-1-ol is C₄H₁₀O.

questions.q: Anhydrous sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime (NaOH and CaO). The gas formed is:
questions.x: This is decarboxylation: CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃. The –COO group leaves as carbonate, so the product has one carbon fewer.

questions.q: In an α-amino acid, the –NH₂ group is attached to:
o: The carbon atom of the –COOH group itself
The carbon atom that is directly bonded to the –COOH group
The carbon farthest from the –COOH group
An oxygen atom of the –COOH group
questions.x: The α-carbon is the carbon next to the carboxyl group, and in α-amino acids it carries both the –NH₂ group and the side chain R.

questions.q: Which of the following is a synthetic adhesive?
questions.x: Urea–methanal resin is made industrially from urea and methanal and is used, for example, to bond plywood. Starch paste, casein glue and animal glue come from natural materials.

questions.q: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 3 units have a scalar product of −6. The angle between them is (cos 120° = −0.5):
questions.x: cos θ = (−6)/(4 × 3) = −0.5, so θ = 120°. A negative scalar product means the angle is more than 90°.

questions.q: A stone is thrown straight up, rises 15 m and falls back into the thrower's hand. The distance travelled and the displacement of the stone are:
questions.x: The stone goes 15 m up and 15 m down, so the distance is 30 m. It ends where it started, so the displacement is zero.

questions.q: A body starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 4 m s⁻². The distance it covers during the 3rd second alone is:
questions.x: Distance in 3 s = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 m; in 2 s = ½ × 4 × 4 = 8 m. During the 3rd second: 18 − 8 = 10 m.

questions.q: The vertical acceleration of a projectile is the same as that of a freely falling body because:
o: In both cases the only force acting is the body's weight
Air resistance acts upward on both
questions.x: Ignoring air resistance, weight is the only force on each, so each accelerates downward at g. A projectile does have horizontal velocity, but that does not affect its vertical acceleration.

questions.q: A ball thrown straight up does NOT move as a two-dimensional projectile because:
o: Gravity does not act on it while rising
Its acceleration changes direction at the top
Its initial velocity has no horizontal component
questions.x: With no horizontal velocity component, the ball moves only along a vertical line, so its motion is one-dimensional.

questions.q: A car moving at 8 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² for 4 s. Its velocity at the end of this time is:
questions.x: v = u + at = 8 + 3 × 4 = 20 m s⁻¹. 12 m s⁻¹ is only the gain in velocity, without the initial 8 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A car travels 40 km due east in 1 h and then 20 km due west in the next 1 h. Its average speed and average velocity for the 2 h are:
o: 30 km h⁻¹ and 30 km h⁻¹ east
10 km h⁻¹ and 10 km h⁻¹ east
30 km h⁻¹ and 10 km h⁻¹ east
questions.x: Average speed = 60 km ÷ 2 h = 30 km h⁻¹. Net displacement = 40 − 20 = 20 km east, so average velocity = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 km h⁻¹ east.

questions.q: A table top is taken as the zero level. A book resting on a shelf higher than the table top has a potential energy that is:
o: Always equal to its kinetic energy
questions.x: PE = mgh with h measured from the zero level. The book is above the table top, so h and PE are positive; below the table top PE would be negative.

questions.q: A porter holds a 20 kg suitcase still above the ground for 5 minutes and feels tired. The work he does on the suitcase is:
o: Zero, because the suitcase has no displacement
questions.x: Work needs displacement. The suitcase does not move, so no work is done on it; the tiredness is due to energy used inside his muscles.

questions.q: When the brakes of a moving car are applied and it stops, its kinetic energy is mainly converted into:
o: Heat in the brakes and tyres
questions.x: The brakes stop the car by friction. The work done against friction changes the kinetic energy into heat in the brake parts, tyres and road.

questions.q: A wheel makes 2.5 revolutions. The angle it turns through, in degrees, is:
questions.x: Each revolution is 360°, so 2.5 × 360° = 900°.

questions.q: A sphere of mass 2 × 10⁻³ kg falls through a liquid at a steady speed. Ignoring upthrust and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the drag force on it is:
o: Zero, because the speed is steady
questions.x: At steady (terminal) speed the net force is zero, so drag = weight = mg = 2 × 10⁻³ × 10 = 2 × 10⁻² N. A steady speed means balanced forces, not zero drag.

questions.q: Two solid spheres of the same material fall through the same viscous liquid. One has 8 times the mass of the other. Using v_t ∝ r² (ignoring upthrust), the ratio of the heavier sphere's terminal velocity to the lighter one's is:
questions.x: Mass ∝ r³ for the same material, so 8 times the mass means twice the radius. Since v_t ∝ r², the terminal velocity is 2² = 4 times as large.

questions.q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe. By how much is the pressure lower at a point where its speed is 6 m s⁻¹ than at a point where its speed is 2 m s⁻¹?
questions.x: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (36 − 4) = 1.6 × 10⁴ Pa. Leaving out the ½ gives 3.2 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.q: In steady circulation, the volume of blood leaving the heart per second equals the total volume flowing through all the capillaries per second. This follows from:
questions.x: The continuity equation is the conservation of mass: blood (nearly incompressible) cannot accumulate or vanish anywhere in the system in steady flow.

questions.q: A string 0.9 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in three loops at 300 Hz. The speed of the waves on the string is:
questions.x: Three loops make 1.5 wavelengths, so λ = 0.9/1.5 = 0.6 m. v = fλ = 300 × 0.6 = 180 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A stationary wave is given this name because:
o: Its particles do not vibrate at all
It can exist only in a solid
Its wave pattern does not move along the medium
It carries energy at a steady speed
questions.x: In a stationary wave the loops stay in place; the particles still vibrate, but the crests do not travel along the medium.

questions.q: Air at a certain temperature has density 1.4 kg m⁻³ when its pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Taking γ = 1.4 for air, Laplace's corrected value for the speed of sound is about:
questions.x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 10⁵ / 1.4) = √(10⁵) ≈ 316 m s⁻¹. Leaving out γ (Newton's formula) gives about 267 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: In general, sound travels:
o: Fastest in gases and slowest in solids
Fastest in solids and slowest in gases
Fastest in liquids and slowest in solids
At the same speed in solids, liquids and gases
questions.x: Solids are far more elastic than liquids, and liquids far more than gases, which outweighs their greater density. So sound is usually fastest in solids and slowest in gases.

questions.q: For a mechanical wave to travel through a material, the material must have:
questions.x: Elasticity gives the restoring force that pulls displaced particles back, and inertia (mass) makes them overshoot and pass the motion on. These properties of the medium carry mechanical waves.

questions.q: In a longitudinal wave, the distance from the centre of the first compression to the centre of the fifth compression is 2.0 m. The wavelength is:
questions.x: From the first to the fifth compression there are 4 wavelengths, so λ = 2.0/4 = 0.5 m. Dividing by 5 (0.4 m) is the usual mistake.

questions.q: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1 × 10⁵ Pa from 2 litres to 5 litres while absorbing 800 J of heat. The change in its internal energy is (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³):
questions.x: Work done by the gas = PΔV = 1 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. ΔU = Q − W = 800 − 300 = +500 J.

questions.q: In Joule's experiments on the mechanical equivalent of heat, the amount of work that produced the same heating as 1 calorie was about:
questions.x: Joule found that about 4.2 J of mechanical work gives the same heating as 1 calorie of heat, showing that heat and work are both forms of energy transfer.

questions.q: A small sphere carries +2 μC. Its potential at a spot 60 cm away is: (take k as 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
questions.x: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.6 = 1.8 × 10⁴ / 0.6 = 3 × 10⁴ V. Dividing by r² would give 5 × 10⁴ V.

questions.q: Near the middle of a very large, uniformly charged flat plate, the electric field is:
o: Uniform in both magnitude and direction
Strongest at the plate and falling off as 1/r²
questions.x: Away from the edges, an infinite charged plate produces a uniform field perpendicular to its surface. The 1/r² fall-off belongs to a point charge.

questions.q: A charge of 0.5 C gains 6 J of energy when it is moved between two points. The potential difference between the points is:
questions.x: V = W/q = 6 / 0.5 = 12 V. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 3 V.

questions.q: A resistor carries 2 A when 10 V is applied across it. If the voltage is raised to 25 V at the same temperature, the current becomes:
questions.x: R = V/I = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 Ω, which stays the same. New current = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 A.

questions.q: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a 6 Ω resistor. The power dissipated in it is:
questions.x: Current I = V/R = 2 A. Power = VI = 12 × 2 = 24 W (or V²/R = 144 ÷ 6). 72 W comes from multiplying V by R.

questions.q: In a mass spectrometer, an ion (2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a 0.5 T field perpendicularly at 4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Its circular path has radius:
Using F = qvB, the tesla can also be written as:
questions.x: B = F/(qv), so its unit is N/(C × m s⁻¹) = N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹.

questions.q: The primary and secondary coils of a transformer are wound on one common iron core so that:
o: Nearly all the changing flux of the primary also links the secondary
The two coils are electrically connected to each other
Direct current can pass from one coil to the other
The core can store the electrical energy
questions.x: The shared core guides the alternating flux from the primary through the secondary, giving good mutual induction. The coils are not electrically joined.

questions.q: The SI unit of capacitive and inductive reactance is the:
questions.x: Reactance is an opposition to AC, V/I, like resistance, so it is measured in ohms. The farad and henry are units of capacitance and inductance.

questions.q: In an unbiased PN junction, the electric field across the depletion region points:
o: From the p-side to the n-side
From the n-side to the p-side
Along the junction, parallel to it
Nowhere, because the field is zero
questions.x: The n-side of the depletion region holds positive ions and the p-side holds negative ions, so the field points from the positive n-side towards the negative p-side.

questions.q: One electronvolt, a unit often used for photon energies, is equal to:
questions.x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moved through 1 V: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.q: In hydrogen the n = 3 level is at −1.51 eV and the n = 2 level is at −3.4 eV. An electron dropping from n = 3 to n = 2 emits a photon of energy:
questions.x: Photon energy = E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.4) = 1.89 eV. This is the red Balmer line; adding the magnitudes (4.91 eV) is a sign error.

questions.q: An isotope has a half-life of 5 years. What fraction of a sample has decayed after 15 years?
questions.x: 15 years is 3 half-lives, so 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8 remains and 7/8 has decayed. 1/8 is the fraction left, not decayed.

questions.q: Last Friday the medical students held a blood donation camp in the college hall. Donors had to be between eighteen and sixty years old and weigh at least fifty kilograms. Each donor's haemoglobin was checked first. Seventy-two people came, but twelve were turned away, most of them because their haemoglobin was too low. Every donor was given juice and biscuits and asked to rest for fifteen minutes. Which statement is NOT true according to the passage?
o: Sixty people gave blood at the camp
Donors had to weigh at least fifty kilograms
Most of the people turned away were under eighteen
Each donor's haemoglobin was checked first
questions.x: The passage says most of those turned away had low haemoglobin, not that they were too young. Seventy-two came and twelve were turned away, so sixty gave blood.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "In the photograph, Sara is sitting ___ Ali and Hamza."
questions.x: 'Between' is used for a position separating two people or things; 'among' is for more than two.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "After the doctor's warning, Sara stopped ___ sweets altogether."
questions.x: 'Stop + gerund' means to give up an activity, which fits the doctor's warning; 'stop + to-infinitive' would mean pausing in order to eat.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "First, wash your hands with soap. ___, dry them with a clean towel."
questions.x: The steps follow one another in order, so a sequence word, 'Next', is needed.

questions.q: In "Bilal admitted taking the money from the drawer", the gerund phrase 'taking the money from the drawer' is:
questions.x: The gerund phrase answers 'admitted what?', so it is the object of the verb.

questions.q: Which sentence uses commas to show that Hamza has only ONE sister?
o: Hamza's sister Ayesha is a doctor.
Hamza's sister, Ayesha, is a doctor.
Hamza's, sister Ayesha is a doctor.
Hamza's sister, Ayesha is, a doctor.
questions.x: Commas around 'Ayesha' mark extra, non-essential information, showing there is only one sister; without commas the name picks out one sister among several.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Each of the girls carried ___ own water bottle on the trip."
questions.x: 'Each' is singular and refers to girls, so the possessive determiner is 'her'; 'hers' cannot stand before a noun.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "Somebody ____ left the tap running in the laboratory."
questions.x: Indefinite pronouns such as somebody, someone and everybody are singular, so the verb is 'has left'.

questions.q: Identify the error in this sentence: "Ayesha is senior than me by two years in college."
o: 'by two years' should be 'from two years'
'in college' should be 'at the college of'
questions.x: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior are followed by 'to', not 'than'. The rest of the sentence is correct.

questions.q: Hamza's mother tells him: "Take an umbrella; the weather report says it will rain this afternoon." Which assumption is she making?
o: The weather report is reasonably reliable
Hamza does not own an umbrella
questions.x: Her advice only makes sense if she trusts the forecast. She does not suggest it always rains, and she assumes Hamza can take an umbrella, not that he lacks one.

questions.q: Every member of group P also belongs to group Q. A few members of group R do not belong to group Q. What can be concluded for certain?
o: Some members of R are not in P
Some members of P are not in R
No member of R is in P
Some members of Q are not in P
questions.x: Every P is a Q, so anything outside Q cannot be in P. The members of R that are outside Q are therefore outside P.

questions.q: What comes next in the letter series B, C, E, G, K, M, ?
questions.x: The letters stand at positions 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, which are the prime numbers. The next prime is 17, which is Q.

questions.q: Three facts are given: some P are Q, every Q is R, and no R is S. Which statement must be true?
questions.x: The P that are Q are also R, and no R is S, so those P are not S. Other P may or may not be S, so 'No P is S' does not follow; no Q can be S.

questions.q: Zara is facing east. She turns to her left. Which direction is she facing now?
questions.x: A left turn is 90 degrees anticlockwise; from east this brings her to face north.

questions.q: Danish, Ehsan, Faiza, Gul and Hassan each visit the library on a different day from Monday to Friday. Danish goes on Thursday. Ehsan goes the day before Danish. Faiza goes on a day after Danish. Gul goes on an earlier day than Hassan. Who goes on Tuesday?
questions.x: Ehsan is Wednesday and Faiza Friday. Monday and Tuesday remain, and Gul is earlier than Hassan, so Gul is Monday and Hassan Tuesday.

questions.q: Statement: A survey finds that students who read books for pleasure write better essays. Courses of action: I. The college library should add more interesting books for general reading. II. Essay writing should be removed from the syllabus. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The finding suggests that encouraging reading improves writing, so action I follows. Removing essays ignores the finding entirely.

questions.q: Ali's phone battery lasted a full day when the phone was new, but two years later it runs out in a few hours, though he uses the phone in the same way. What is the most likely cause?
o: The phone's screen has become larger
The phone's camera has been damaged
The battery has aged and now holds less charge
questions.x: Rechargeable batteries slowly lose capacity with age and use. Since his use has not changed, an ageing battery best explains the shorter life.

questions.q: Some people believe that cold weather on its own gives people the flu. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Flu is more common in summer than in winter
Cold weather makes people stay indoors and sleep
Flu is caused by a virus, so a person catches it only after being exposed to the virus
questions.x: Influenza is an infection caused by a virus. Cold weather alone cannot cause it without the virus being passed on.
